name: Greater Toronto
note: Fishing locations for this city. Downloaded with the city's map, not bundled with the app. Derived from the records that used to sit in src/App.jsx - see tools/build-spots.mjs.

spots.name: Bluffer's Park
spots.water: Lake Ontario — below the Scarborough Bluffs
spots.blurb: Marina and pier under the Bluffs, with deep water close to shore. One of the best known shore spots in the city, and reachable without a car.
spots.hazards: Deep water close in below the Bluffs, and the cliff face above is actively eroding - stay off the base of it.
spots.tip: Spring and autumn are the shore seasons, when migratory fish are close. Reachable without a car, which is rare here.

spots.name: Humber River at the Old Mill
spots.blurb: The lower Humber through the parkland above the marshes. Best known for the autumn salmon run and spring steelhead; quiet the rest of the year.
spots.hazards: Urban river that rises fast and dirty after rain. Do not wade it on a rising level.
spots.tip: Known for the autumn salmon run and spring steelhead, and quiet in between. Fish it in the week either side of rain.

spots.name: Toronto Harbour & Harbourfront
spots.blurb: Sheltered water in the middle of the city, with railings and boardwalk for much of it. Warmer and slower than the open lake.
spots.hazards: Boat and ferry traffic, and vertical walls with deep water. Warmer and slower than the open lake.
spots.tip: Sheltered when the lake is unfishable, which is its real value. Carp, pike and panfish rather than migratory fish.

spots.name: Rouge Beach & the Rouge River mouth
spots.blurb: A river mouth and marsh at the eastern edge of the city, inside Rouge National Urban Park. River, marsh and lake shore in one place.
spots.hazards: Marsh margins are soft and the river mouth shifts. Inside a national urban park, so check what is permitted where.
spots.tip: River, marsh and lake shore in one place. The mouth is the interesting part when fish are moving.

spots.name: Credit River, Port Credit
spots.water: Credit River — lower river and mouth
spots.blurb: The lower Credit through Port Credit to the lake. A well known migratory river with parkland access along much of the lower reach.
spots.hazards: A popular migratory river, which means crowds at the peak and etiquette that matters. Slippery bedrock in the lower river.
spots.tip: One of the best-known migratory rivers on this lake. Go early, and leave the spawning gravel alone.

spots.name: Don River at the mouth
spots.blurb: The lower Don where it meets the harbour, hard against the city. An urban river in the fullest sense — concrete, rail and traffic — and still a migratory route, with fish running it in autumn and spring past all of it.
spots.hazards: Urban river with hard edges, storm outfalls and no easy way out of the water. It rises very fast after rain. Consumption advisories apply — check before keeping anything.
spots.tip: Autumn, after rain, for migratory fish. The rest of the year it is a carp river and a surprisingly good one.

spots.name: The Ship Channel
spots.blurb: The straight industrial cut in the Port Lands, deep-walled and still. Unlovely, close to the middle of the city, and holds fish precisely because nobody goes there to look at it.
spots.hazards: Vertical walls with no ladders and deep water right at the edge. Working port traffic. Nothing to break a fall and nothing to climb out on — do not fish it alone.
spots.tip: Vertical structure fishing: drop straight down the wall rather than casting out. Everything here lives against the concrete.

spots.name: Mimico Creek at the lake
spots.water: Mimico Creek — mouth at Lake Ontario
spots.blurb: A small creek entering Lake Ontario in the west end, with a park along the last stretch. Small water and a busy shoreline, but the mouth does what every mouth does and concentrates what is moving through.
spots.hazards: Urban creek that floods hard and fast after rain — it has killed people. Do not be in it or beside it when the water is rising. Storm outfalls throughout.
spots.tip: Autumn migratory fish at the mouth. Watch the weather rather than the water: this creek rises faster than you can walk out of it.

spots.name: Black Creek at the Humber
spots.water: Black Creek — tributary of the Humber
spots.blurb: A small tributary meeting the Humber in the west end, with trail access along much of it. Shallow, urban and overlooked, and the confluence is the reason to come.
spots.hazards: Flashy urban creek — it rises fast and dirty after rain. Soft, undercut banks. Storm outfalls, and water quality to match after a storm.
spots.tip: Fish the confluence pool where the creek meets the Humber. That one spot is worth more than the rest of the creek together.

spots.name: Don River East Branch at Taylor Creek
spots.water: Don River East Branch — inland reach
spots.blurb: The east branch well inland, running through a long ravine park with trail access the whole way. Small, clear and shaded — a ravine stream inside a city of three million, which is the whole point of it.
spots.hazards: Ravine creek: it rises very fast in rain and the banks are steep and slippery. Shared-use trails throughout. Water quality is urban — do not eat what you catch here.
spots.tip: A walking fishery. Small spinner, light line, and work upstream through the ravine covering pools as you go.
